meta.title: Have an idea? Make the people who build it your partners — instead of chasing investors | 1lev1
meta.description: Another way to start a business: instead of decks, investors and salaries you have to raise, whoever works on the idea becomes a partner by what they contributed. Try it now and see your idea as a rikma.

hero.h1: Instead of chasing investors — make the people who build the business your partners
hero.sub: The usual road: a deck, investors, then salaries for employees. The rikma road: the people who would have been your first hires join as partners, and each gets a share by what they actually contributed. Less money to raise, fewer contracts, and more people who care that it works.
hero.ctaTry: See my idea as a rikma
hero.artAlt: On the left, a founder alone holds a pitch board in front of a closed door, waiting. On the right, an idea bulb stitches pink threads out to four partners, with a heart above it.

roads.title: Two ways to start a business
roads.sub: Both are legitimate. The difference is who funds the start, and who benefits when it works.
roads.usual_r1: Months of decks and investor meetings before you have worked a single day on the idea.
roads.usual_r2: The investor takes a large share, and the people who build the business get a salary.
roads.usual_r3: Every employee is a monthly cost, so you need to raise more money to hire more people.
roads.usual_r4: Decisions are made at the top, and the team executes.
roads.usual_r5: When the money runs out, the business stops.
roads.rikma_r1: You start working in the first week: publish missions, and whoever fits joins.
roads.rikma_r2: Everyone who builds the business — with work, money or equipment — gets a share by their contribution.
roads.rikma_r3: A partner does not cost a salary. You only raise money for what cannot come in through partnership.
roads.rikma_r4: Whoever sees a need opens a mission, and the partners approve. You are not the bottleneck.
roads.rikma_r5: The business keeps moving without a big budget, because everyone invests in their own share.
roads.fit: It fits best when the business is built mostly from people's work and skills, and when you prefer committed partners over salaried staff. An investor can still join — as a partner, by the money they bring.

demo.title: See how your idea becomes a rikma
demo.sub: Describe the idea in a few sentences. Our AI breaks it into missions, the resources you lack and what the business will sell — and shows each partner's share.
demo.label: What is the idea?
demo.placeholder: For example: I want to open a neighbourhood café that doubles as a coworking and workshop space. I have management experience; I need a barista, an interior designer and someone who can market...
demo.ex1Text: I want to open a neighbourhood café that doubles as a coworking space and hosts workshops in the evenings. I have management experience, and I need a barista, an interior designer, someone who can market on social media, and a suitable place.
demo.ex2Text: I want to build an app that connects dog owners in the neighbourhood for shared walks and dog-sitting. I have the idea and community connections; I need a developer, a UX designer and someone to build the first community.
demo.ex3Text: I want to build a retreat center with lodging for fifty people, a kitchen with a vegetable garden, a workshop hall and a spa, which facilitators can also rent for events. We need to find land, funding, and people for building, food and content.
demo.disclaimer: This is a reduced preview our AI prepares from your description, and nothing is saved. On the site the draft is fuller: you edit every mission, hours and rates, invite partners and watch the split update.
demo.shareNote: The percentage is the starting share of whoever takes the mission, if each mission is taken by a different partner. In a real rikma the share updates by the hours actually approved, and includes money and equipment too.

demo.fuller: In the full draft every row is editable, and you can invite partners right away.

gap.title: Where ideas like this usually stall
gap.sub: Not for lack of people or will. Most initiatives stop at the same four points:
gap.g1: A WhatsApp group full of enthusiasm, and nobody knows what exactly their task is this week.
gap.g2: One brings money, one brings equipment, one puts in a year of work — and there is no fair way to compare them.
gap.g3: A partnership agreement costs a lot, takes months, and freezes what was agreed on day one — exactly while everything is still changing.
gap.g4: The founder becomes the bottleneck: every decision, every idea and every step goes through them, until they burn out.

steps.title: How it works, step by step
steps.s1_b: In your own words. The AI breaks it into a draft: missions, missing resources, and what the business will sell. Everything stays editable.
steps.s2_b: Each mission with a scope in hours and a rate, each resource with a value. Whoever fits joins through a mission — no job interview and no employment contract.
steps.s3_t: Every contribution is recorded and becomes a share
steps.s3_b: Work hours, money, equipment and space — all measured in the same units and approved by the partners. Everyone sees the same numbers.
steps.s4_t: Any partner can move things forward
steps.s4_b: A partner who sees a need proposes a new mission, a resource or an approach to an outside party, and the rikma approves. The business moves even when you are not in the room.
steps.s5_t: Decide by consent, at the pace you set
steps.s5_b: You can approve, discuss or make a counter-proposal. A proposal nobody answered within the time you set is approved. No endless meetings.
steps.s6_t: When income arrives, it is split by contribution
steps.s6_b: Every sale is recorded, and the profit is divided among the partners by the shares they built up. No arguing over fifty-fifty.

pillars.title: What saves you time and headaches
pillars.transparency_b: Every partner sees what was done, who contributed what, and how it translates into their share. Fewer questions, fewer suspicions.
pillars.initiative_t: It is not all on you
pillars.initiative_b: Missions are opened by whoever sees the need. You set the direction; you do not manage every detail.
pillars.order_b: Every mission has a scope, a rate, an owner and its own conversation. It is clear what is open, what is in progress and what is done.
pillars.contracts_b: The agreements themselves are recorded: who committed to what, at what rate, and who approved. They update along the way instead of freezing on day one.

doubts.title: Questions founders ask
doubts.q1_q: No agreement at all? Isn't that risky?
doubts.q1_a: The agreements do not disappear — they are recorded in the system: who committed to what, at what rate, and who approved. That is a clearer basis than most agreements, and it updates along the way. If at some point you want a formal agreement as well, it is written from the data rather than from scratch.
doubts.q2_q: How do you compare someone who brings money with someone who brings work?
doubts.q2_a: Every contribution gets a value: an hour at the agreed rate, money at its amount, equipment and space at their worth. It all goes into the same account, so at any moment you can see each person's share.
doubts.q3_q: What if a partner disappears halfway?
doubts.q3_a: A mission that is not moving does not stay stuck: the rikma can propose releasing it, and whoever holds it gets time to respond. What they already contributed stays theirs, and the mission opens up again for someone else.
doubts.q4_q: Do I lose control over my idea?
doubts.q4_a: The direction and the values are written into the rikma from the start, and whoever joins, joins them. Decisions are shared, but nobody can impose a veto — not against you either. And your work as founders counts like any other contribution.
doubts.q5_q: And if I still need an investor?
doubts.q5_a: No problem. An investor joins the rikma like any partner: the money they bring is recorded as a contribution, and they get a share by its value. The difference is that they are not the only one who gets a share — the people who built the business do too.
